This paper examines the allocation of indivisible goods among agents with additive valuations, focusing on envy-freeness up to one item (EF1). It highlights existing algorithms that guarantee proportional (PF) outcomes under certain monotonicity assumptions and discusses their implications for EF1 allocations. Additionally, it explores efficient approximation methods for these solutions and discusses open inquiries within this research framework.

In the source domain, access to complete scene semantic labels is available; conversely, the target domain relies on only a sparse set of sparse annotations. The low surface brightness (LSB) spiral UGC 8839 exhibits a puzzlingly high concentration of star formation at its periphery, a phenomenon this study seeks to explain via three-dimensional radiative transfer simulations of the galaxy's interstellar medium. The model accounts for the galaxy's observed mass distribution, structural parameters, and kinematic data. The results suggest that the massive spiral arms act as compressive regions, triggering extensive star formation in their outer extents. Additionally, the model indicates that the galaxy likely possesses a flared disc structure; consequently, star-forming activity occurs not only within the observable surface but also in the unseen upper layers of the disc during this evolutionary phase. Radiative feedback from newly formed stars is shown to be a critical factor, enabling the sustained high star-formation rates observed in the outer regions. Ultimately, these mechanisms offer a framework for understanding star formation dynamics in UGC 8839 and similar systems.

Paleo-detectors, such as those currently under development at the Proton Radiation Analysis Detector (PRAD)/paleo-detector (PRAD/paleo-detector) facility, represent a pioneering concept in direct WIMP detection. These paleo-detectors offer a dual function: they serve as standard WIMP sensors during their deployment and, after exposure to high neutron fluxes, serve as sensitive detectors for WIMPs with lower cross-sections for extended durations. This dual nature allows paleo-detectors to identify signals from WIMPs with lower scattering rates, which would otherwise require more sensitive experiments or longer observation times. By leveraging the dual function, paleo-detectors can detect signals from WIMPs with lower scattering rates, which would otherwise require more sensitive experiments or longer observation times. These capabilities make paleo-detectors a unique tool for exploring parameter spaces inaccessible to conventional sensors.

This study presents the concept of update pattern leakage as a novel risk in modern encrypted databases. It formalizes the definition and security model of DP-Sync specifically regarding data processing (DP) update patterns, while outlining a corresponding DP-Sync framework that upgrades current encrypted database systems to support DP-Sync through DP-compatible updates. The proposed protocol ensures strong protection for the full data evolution history on the stored structures by applying differential privacy principles governing how data owners perform their local data sync operations.

Minimally invasive surgeries allow for internal anatomical visualization and intervention via external access points using endoscopic tools, facilitating procedures such as organ removal, repair, and transplantation. If endoscopic image quality deteriorates or the surgeon loses situational awareness, these advantages are negated, potentially necessitating a conversion to open surgery. This study focuses on detecting contact events during endoscopic cardiac surgery to enhance surgical safety. We introduce a learning-based framework that leverages multi-view endoscopic video streams to identify the specific view closest to a contact event. We evaluated our framework using datasets compiled from Karl Storz endoscopic videos of cardiac pig lung lobectomy and splenectomy operations performed at Karolinska University Hospital. Experimental results demonstrate the framework's capacity to deliver real-time contact inference across both healthy and pathological tissue conditions using the available video material. Expanding the dataset with additional cases will further enable robust generalization in a clinical setting.

This research introduces a novel measurement equation for threshold selection within Realized-GARCH models. The developed framework integrates a nonlinear threshold regression scheme to capture the leverage effect and represent the simultaneous linkage between observed realized metrics and latent volatility. Estimation of the model utilizes Bayesian Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods, with its credibility tested through simulations. Further validation involving the application of the suggested measurement equation within Realized-GARCH variants is conducted via an empirical analysis, specifically forecasting the 1% Value-at-Risk and Expected Shortfall for six stock indices using two varying out-of-sample durations. The study demonstrates that the proposed methodology generates comparable tail risk forecasts when benchmarked against traditional GARCH and Realized-GARCH models.

Global pulsar timing arrays are currently investigating for a nano-Hertz gravitational wave background signal potentially sourced by stochastic cosmic strings; although this search has not yet yielded a definitive detection, analysis of existing data suggests it is worthwhile to extract individual GW imprints from the timing residuals of stellar-mass black hole (BH) mergers. We evaluate the signature cosmic strings would produce on a merging BH pair, focusing on how merger event parameters modulate any resulting detectable effect. Our findings focus on three key points: first, a stochastic network of cosmic strings is unlikely to generate a strong GW signal in an isolated merger; second, the creation of long, stable strings through semi-classical graviton decay during the early universe is constrained to produce no more than $O(10^{-2} \Omega_{\rm DE})$ of the dark energy density today; and third, a sufficiently strong coupling between the GW field and cosmic matter could leave a distinct, detectable trace of the merger within pulsar data.

We have undertaken a systematic investigation into the correlation functions of pion currents composed of two quarks using lattice QCD. Excellent signals were observed for all pertinent Wick contractions, except for a single instance. We analyzed the dependency of our findings on quark mass to evaluate whether correlations among quarks and antiquark indices significantly influence the results. Furthermore, we evaluated the physical relevance of these data by comparing them to correlations derived from currents that generate the same quark-mass-independent current.

The regulation of protoplanetary disk evolution relies on analyzing how accretion rates scale with star and disk attributes; however, utilizing data from the ALESS 30 survey reveals a key discrepancy. While the widely adopted linear correlation between disk mass and central stellar mass predicts specific accretion rates, the observed values deviate significantly by an order of magnitude or more. These predictions, derived from 21 cm continuum and molecular emission observations across multiple phases of ALESS 30's evolution, highlight an order-of-moment difference between expected and actual behavior. Consequently, simply applying the standard mass-relationship fails to model these systems accurately, suggesting that accretion dynamics must be modeled as a distinct function of stellar and disk evolutionary phases. Ultimately, this finding underscores the necessity of developing an explicit empirical model of formation to effectively constrain physical accretion mechanisms.

This study investigates how individuals approach income redistribution in contexts where uncertainty surrounds the extent to which luck determines opportunities and results. By querying participants from a U.S.-demographically representative study group, we found that most people condition their views on redistribution regarding opportunity and outcome uncertainty regarding luck. Furthermore, introducing this uncertainty tends to promote the view that income should be redistributed. Our third key result demonstrates that these findings cannot be explained by a standard two-factor model of inequality aversion and risk tolerance; instead, we offer an alternative framework based on expected utility and "incredulity," which defines luck incredulity as the degree to which people disbelieve that luck drives worker opportunities and outcomes. Our final recommendation suggests that future research into the public's views on economic policy should incorporate behavioral elements beyond simple risk and inequality preferences.

In summary (paraphrased): We examine how people decide on income redistribution when it is uncertain whether luck dictates worker outcomes and opportunities. Data from a U.S. representative sample indicates that individuals largely base such decisions on these uncertainties, and that highlighting them encourages support for redistribution. While a model combining inequality aversion and risk tolerance fails to capture our third finding about the role of "luck incredulity," we provide a structure relying instead on expected utility and this specific measure of disbelief. Finally, to fully understand views on economic strategy, researchers should consider behavioral factors in their models.

This paper investigates degree stable maps, forgetful transformations of partial flag manifolds, and their connections to specific Schubert varieties within these spaces. For any partial flag manifold $M$ within a complete flag manifold $F_n$, there exists a associated covering map $p_M: F_n \to M$. We demonstrate that the set of degree stable maps into $M$, denoted $\degStbMap{M}{d}$, forms a collection of bundles over $M$ where each fiber corresponds to $d$ copies of the fibers of $p_M$. Furthermore, for any irreducible map $\phi$ in $\degStbMap{M}{d}$, its composition $p_M \circ \phi$ defines a correspondence between the boundaries of $M$ and $d$ copies of the boundaries of $F_n$. In the context of an arbitrary irreducible map $\phi: S^k \to M$ belonging to $\degStbMap{M}{d}$, we examine the closure of the image under $p \circ \circ$, identifying it as a specific subvariety of $F_n$ with dimensions no greater than those predicted by the degree of the map composed with $p_M$. Finally, when $\phi$ is the composition $p_M \circ \circ$, we determine the precise dimension of the resulting subvariety of $F_n$.

Building contemporary machine learning (ML) applications relies heavily on data-centric approaches, where engineers refine the efficacy of trained algorithms by strategically modifying the training environment and data flows. While conceptually straightforward, accurately computing these refinements remains a persistent hurdle. This computation challenge hinders the ability to scale ML operations in real-world scenarios. To address this, we propose a novel framework for calculating Shapley values specifically for modifications in ML training data. Our method capitalizes on the symmetry inherent within data-centric shapley calculations to determine valid factorized formulas. We then derive efficient algorithms for computing these factorized formulas, facilitating the application of shapley values to large-scale ML datasets. Evaluations across three distinct models and three extensive datasets demonstrate a speedup in our calculations ranging from hundreds to tens of thousands of times faster, relative to existing methods. Consequently, these capabilities empower data stakeholders to analyze economic and fairness-related queries regarding their training data with greater transparency. Our open-source implementation, available at https://github.com/shapley-ml/shapley-ml, serves as a practical tool for these insights.

This study examines potential links among core radio source counts, stellar encounter rates, and either masses or half-light radii (encounter rates) for 14 Milky Way globular clusters. Utilizing the Arecibo and Parkes 74 MHz data, we identified 444 radio sources associated with the clusters through careful subtraction of the average background source density. By analyzing the most likely masses of black holes paired with typical companion stars required to generate these source counts, we evaluated their impact on the dynamical evolution of the clusters. Radio source counts in these systems notably correlate with both stellar mass and half-light radius, as predicted by a binary black hole formation model. Assuming that the final destruction of clusters occurs upon the radio-inactive merger of binary black holes, we estimate a lower bound for the final destruction mass of each cluster based on its radio emission. For the subset of clusters where $N_{Radio} \ge 1$, the calculated minimum masses are significantly lower than, or comparable to, the currently known masses of those clusters. Moreover, our estimated lower limits for the final destruction masses align well with the final masses observed in radio-inactive systems, suggesting that radio-active emission serves as a reliable tracer for binary black hole formation and the subsequent binary-to-single conversion process.

Graph analysis has proven vital for understanding and predicting the behavior of complex systems; still, a significant portion of real-world systems require hypergraph modeling rather than traditional graphs to be accurately forecasted. A hyperedge connects multiple nodes, and sparsely populated hyperedges drive phenomena like epidemic spreading. Due to their long tails, such connections are often ignored in computational processes. Furthermore, the significance of hyperedges is context-dependent and fluctuates dynamically, necessitating adaptive management.

We propose an innovative framework utilizing adaptive importance hyperedges (AIH) to compute and assess the stability of epidemic thresholds and other outcomes related to hypergraphs. Our approach is grounded in a probabilistic framework that assigns connection likelihoods based on the sparsity of hyperedges. This ensures computational efficiency by focusing exclusively on the most probable multi-node interactions within the hyperedges. Consequently, this method facilitates modeling and analyzing spreading dynamics on both deterministic and stochastic hypergraphs. Extensive tests across diverse scenarios confirm the framework's efficacy and superiority compared to current approaches.

This work introduces a robust metric for characterizing unidirectional emission in microcavity lasers. While Shannon entropy applied to far-field distributions—calculated within polar coordinates to ascertain directional symmetry and its stability against parameter-induced deformationsoffers superior performance compared to conventional methods—a phenomenologically defined divergence angle based on full width at half maximum (FWHM) often falters when analyzing structures with multiple peaks. In contrast, Shannon entropy applied to the Cartesian semi-marginal probability of far-field profiles achieves comparable results for standard cases but uniquely provides reliability for emitting profiles featuring complicated peak structures.

We examine how a thermal alkali-vapor sample (temperated between 350 K and 550 K) coherently scatters laser light, with atomic separation distances in the vapor varying from approximately 35 Å to 10 Å as a function of temperature. By analyzing atomic coherence and polarization effects, we identify that photons scattered by individual atoms lose atomic-resolution spectral features when the vapor's average atomic spacing ($d$) approaches or falls below the optical wavelength ($\lambda$), specifically when $d \lesssim \lambda$. This phenomenon enables the determination of number densities ($n = 1/d^3$) with an uncertainty of roughly $\pm 10^{10}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-3}$, notwithstanding broad intrinsic variations within the vapor column. Additionally, this sensitive response to density fluctuations enables the instrument's use as an ultra-stable interferometric reference, supporting applications in optical frequency conversion, spectroscopy, and the generation of synergistic outer-scheme entangled states involving both light and atomic degrees of freedom.

Offline multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) focuses on learning effective multi-agent strategies from stored, uninteractive agent trajectories for transfer. A critical real-world scenario in offline MARL involves combining policies from different levels of performance—such as merging a high-level expert policy from a single environment with lower-level policies from others—which is crucial for automated team formation with heterogeneous agents. In this work, we focus on symmetric multi-agent settings where all agents share an identical reward function and face a similar challenge of selecting action probabilities based on their respective offline data sources. Our goal is to determine the optimal mixture of these distinct behaviors to maximize the return of the group. We demonstrate that in many cases, a symmetric mean-field formulation serves as a sufficiently accurate approximation for the original multi-agent framework. Leveraging this reduction, we apply standard fixed-point resolution techniques to derive optimal mixing coefficients. Our method guarantees finding the best combination of performance levels in any given symmetric multi-agent Markov decision process. Empirical evaluations across various test cases confirm these findings and highlight the significance of our proposed approach.

We introduce a two- to three-dimensional medical view image registration approach grounded in Convolutional Neural Networks. Most traditional intensity-based methods, which utilize optimization algorithms to maximize image similarity, often yield good outcomes for kilovoltage images; however, due to inferior image quality, these methods typically underperform on megavoltage images with limited capture ranges. To mitigate these deficiencies, this study proposes a Convolutional Neural Network framework. Experiments conducted on a dataset of 50 brain scans yield promising results when benchmarked against conventional registration techniques.

In this section, we explore quantum nonlocality from the perspective of two inertial observers, each sharing entangled correlations with the particle they observe. The result reveals that these shared observers detect distinct quantum states—states possessing differing values for various physical properties—even though they share the same spacetime event. Furthermore, the analysis demonstrates how the observed effects of quantum nonlocality evolve as velocity varies relative to specific inertial frames. The theoretical conclusions have immediate relevance to emerging technologies such as quantum internet infrastructure and high-precision metrology.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence and advanced information technology holds significant promise for improving safety and efficiency in the Internet of Vehicles (IoV) by analyzing vast vehicle datasets. However, centralizing these data poses significant security and privacy risks, alongside concerns over intellectual property. Federated Learning (FL) serves as a robust solution, enabling model training across distributed nodes without exposing raw data. This paper reviews current research on implementing FL in intelligent IoV environments. Key advantages of FL include the creation of a shared global vehicular AI model while keeping individual transport operator and infrastructure (e.g., cellular base stations) control over their specific datasets intact. Additionally, the study explores leveraging FL to build comprehensive maps of geographic and driver behavior patterns. Finally, the authors examine critical challenges regarding security and security mechanisms specifically within IoV-based FL frameworks.

We introduce a feedback encoding methodology rooted in Gaussian mixture modeling (GMMs). Initially, we partition channel channels into clusters using the k-means technique and establish a codebook of GMM parameters, differentiated by cluster. Coordinating and learning in dynamic environments are prevalent across biological and social domains. The sensor employs a phase-detector architecture built from two oscillators with time periods that exhibit a thermal-dependent linear relationship. Magnetic fields observed in A-type stars, white dwarfs, and neutron stars are renowned for their long-term stability and persistence for millions or even billions of years. Theoretical models typically attribute this durability to the stars' highly conductive exteriors, which facilitate stable, self-generated equilibrium currents. This paper investigates the temporal evolution of magnetic fields in highly conductive environments where magnetic diffusion cannot be disregarded. We examine two distinct initial field scenarios: a dipole field and a field concentrated in a localized region. Our findings reveal that the localized field configuration undergoes dynamo-like instability during diffusion, producing magnetic structures on timescales shorter than $10^7$ years, whereas the dipole field remains stable throughout its diffusion process. These results carry significant implications for understanding fields in neutron stars and the accretion disks surrounding them.

The functional renormalization group (FRG) offers a versatile framework for analyzing strongly correlated systems, yet its efficacy relies on the user-supplied ansatz for the irreducible vertex. This work explores the application of the exact flow equation within lattice models, specifically the XY model and the SU(2) lattice gauge model (SUGM). Results demonstrate that a simple ansatz, derived directly from the lattice formulation and inserted into the FRG exact equation, yields plausible phase diagrams that align well with established literature, thereby validating the methodology. Furthermore, these findings suggest that specific approximations to the vertex flow equation are unnecessary. Additionally, this approach facilitates an investigation into order parameter evolution under FRG, yielding results congruent with those of the mean field approximation.

LiDAR point clouds capture detailed 3D representations of extensive areas, facilitating the detection and analysis of hazards, infrastructure, and natural features. Consequently, these data are vital for monitoring the environment, supporting urban development, and enabling disaster preparedness and response. However, traditional manual labeling of such point clouds is resource-intensive and slow. This study introduces PointVQA, a benchmark dataset comprising 1.1 million densely sampled, color-enriched LiDAR scenes across diverse settings. These datasets include over 950,000 textual queries of varying difficulty, query types, and spans, with more than 950,000 queries labeled for evaluation. Based on this benchmark, we propose VicVQA, a two-stage point cloud model that utilizes external vision-language encoders to handle queries of differing scopes. VicVQA achieves a CIDEr score of 54.4 on unlquery, significantly outperforming baseline models. Further analyses explore query complexity, the impact of completion components, and evaluation metrics. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to evaluate and enhance closed-loop vision-language models using large-scale LiDAR data.

The source of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs), a longstanding mystery, can potentially be investigated via high-energy neutrinos generated by cosmic-ray hadrons interacting with an astrophysical source's accretion disk or jet. This paper examines how multi-UHECR hadron beams might alter the disk accretion dynamics around such astronomical objects. The analysis reveals that for realistic parameters, even extensive beams fail to significantly modify accretion or neutrino production mechanisms for standard candles like X-ray binaries, active galactic nuclei (AGN), and gamma-ray bursts. However, it proposes a novel mechanism wherein BEAMING accretion disks enhance both accretion rates and the high-energy neutrino/antineutrino fluxes. Such effects are most prominent around compact binaries comprising two ultramassive stellar objects, offering a compelling explanation for the origins of UHECRs and neutrinos.

The rheology of complex liquids is highly sensitive to interfacial roughness conditions. By correlating stress assessments with visual observations of various moving rough interfaces within dry liquid foams, this study reveals three distinct mechanical regimes: slipplase, stick-slip motion, and anchored soap films. The measured stresses in anchored film regimes exceed those of fully wet, rough, and saturated systems by orders of magnitude. Furthermore, a size-dependent stress increase characterizes the anchored film regime, while the slipplase and stick-slip regimes are modeled as motion-induced capillary pumping processes. This pumping mechanism is regulated by the balance between the pumping force and surface tension forces acting across the collapsed plateaus of the rough surface. Ultimately, the transition between these behaviors is governed by a universal threshold defined as the ratio of a roughness feature's size to the liquid's co length.

In May 2019, the ISIC challenge 2019 was released, inviting submissions for a test dataset comprising dermoscopic images classified into five specific categories of skin cancer types. This challenge featured a test corpus of 259 images, divided into five classes representing various forms of skin cancer, with tasks focused on accurate diagnosis and classification. Our team, DeepSense, submitted results for automatic skin cancer diagnosis and classification among these categories. Our approach utilized a ResNet-50 architecture fine-tuned on a subset of 9,909 images to enhance its ability to classify skin cancer types based on image data. To address potential biases or inconsistencies in certain image categories within the training split, we implemented a weighting strategy based on validation performance. Following feature extraction using the pre-trained model, we established a linear support vector machine (SVM) classifier to finalize output predictions for the target dataset. Evaluation of our method on the challenge's test set demonstrated a macro-averaged F1-score of 0.75. A subsequent ablation study confirmed that combining the weighted fine-tuning approach with the linear SVM classifier yielded superior performance compared to baseline configurations.

This study investigates the stationary fingers arising in a rotating Hele-Shaw cell, focusing on an elastic membrane dividing two fluids of differing densities under external pressure. Analysis focuses on the scenario where the membrane tension exceeds its shear modulus, causing it to behave like a soap film with surface area minimization as the primary driver. The membrane's final shape is determined by a balance between surface forces, external pressure, centrifugal effects, and intrinsic elasticity. The primary method employed is an asymptotic expansion of the membrane profile, which yields a non-linear advection equation for the local height deviation from equilibrium. The derived leading-order solution accurately models finger profiles observed in numerical simulations across various rotation rates. Theoretical results indicate that the onset of fingering instability is promoted by low rotation speeds, high bi-layer immobility (high Saffman-Delbrück number), and conditions where surface energy dominates over elastic modulus. The study concludes by presenting the theoretical prediction of the linear growth rate during the initial instability phase, a prediction subsequently corroborated by detailed numerical simulations.

Attention mechanisms have established themselves as fundamental components of Neural Machine Translation (NMT), fostering a link between emerging words and prior generations. Although extensively utilized, the precise nature of this dependency and the motivations driving the attention process remain poorly understood. We demonstrate that in translation models utilizing linear attention mechanisms, the formation of target words is stochastically conditioned on fixed, hand-crafted sequences of hand-calculated attention weights—therefore deterministically—on prior words, independent of RNN cell states or positional encodings. Beyond this theoretical revelation, we introduce the Attential Transformr Model, offering a novel Attnal Translation Model that converts the opaque Neural Attention mechanism into Neural Linear Regression. This allows for learning the underlying functional mapping from historical inputs to proactive attention weights, facilitating reversible translation. As demonstrated by our findings, this approach yields performance equal or superior to current state-of-the-art translation systems while significantly enhancing performance in few-shot translation scenarios and enabling more reliable alignment of generated sequences with input inputs.

The discrepancy between groundbreaking laboratory discoveries and their implementation in clinical practice has fueled the development of translational medicine, with the aim of accelerating and improving public health. While numerous research frameworks exist, they diverge in details; therefore, this study introduces a formal mathematical model designed to evaluate the efficacy of various frameworks for integrating findings into clinical trials. By representing real-world biology and regulatory protocols through model components, we developed stochastic differential equations incorporating Brownian motion to simulate drug discovery, validation, and clinical trial phases. Our analysis reveals that the proposed concept of 'full translational medicine,' which emphasizes the rapid integration of lab results into early-phase trials, consistently outperforms 'liberal translational medicine'—characterized by lenient pre-trial efficacy standards—across all scenarios. Specifically, leveraging three years of data from the breast cancer drug 'Tamoxifen,' our model demonstrates that the liberal approach delays patient access to curative treatments by an average of 11.5 years relative to the full translational approach.

We examine a coherent dissipative dark fluid framework composed of an ordinary viscous component and a heating component, where heating is defined as internal work done on the fluid by its self-dissipative processes. Within this model, we perform the thermodynamic and thermoeconomic analyses of two specific scenarios: finite-time (irreversible) steady cross-membrane heat and mass transfer, as well as finite-time (irreversible) steady heat and mass filtration driven by simultaneous thermal and concentration gradients on either side of the membrane. Our thermodynamic assessment calculates the rates of entropy production, power, and exergy for these processes, while our economic evaluation determines the costs of time and flow for heated and enriched fluids relative to initial conditions and thermal/mass gradient intensities. Our results indicate that both temporal and financial costs for processing the fluid double as self-dissipation coefficients rise; specifically, higher self-dissipation reduces fluid penetration rates due to lowered velocities and diminishes available work via exergy reduction. Conversely, we observe that higher external driving gradients can partially counteract these increases. These findings offer practical guidance for optimizing the utilization of dark fluids in thermoeconomic applications.

Curiosity serves as a fundamental driver of learning, fostering both creativity and a passion for education. This study examines the role of teacher-induced curiosity in students and explores pedagogical strategies to cultivate it within the classroom. We introduce a novel theoretical framework that categorizes student learning drives into two distinct types: induced curiosity and intrinsic interest. Based on this model, we investigate the optimization of learning activities to promote the development of both. Our work offers a theoretical foundation for understanding student motivation and suggests promising research avenues regarding their integrated dynamics.

Gaussian processes constitute a versatile method for regression, classification, and classification. While significant research exists regarding processes in Euclidean spaces, fewer studies cover scenarios in non-Euclidean settings, such as those defined by undirected graphs. This paper introduces a novel Gaussian process on undirected graphs that integrates functional prior knowledge about the target realization's graph-based properties, specifically its smoothness and structural zero-constraints. We detail the derivation of this graph-based process, providing full specifications for both the prior and posterior when observations are available. To illustrate its practical application and flexibility, we present examples demonstrating how to incorporate various smoothness and zero-constraint formulations. Finally, we compare the performance of graph-based and standard Euclidean processes across several regression tasks, highlighting the advantages of utilizing known graphical prior information to enhance predictive accuracy.

Present monitoring methods primarily rely on inductive loop sensors, surveillance cameras, and mobile sensing technologies. However, these approaches suffer from significant drawbacks, including prohibitive installation expenses, concerns over user privacy, and the inability to capture sustained data from drivers who avoid specific routes due to negative mobile experiences.

This research proposes a Wi-Fi-based sensor system designed to detect the presence and volume of vehicles at designated locations within urban environments. This device operates by analyzing the Exposed and Probed (EAP) protocols associated with WiFi interactions. We present the comprehensive theoretical underpinnings required for the research alongside the implementation framework and algorithmic details. Through empirical simulation, we demonstrate that the MFSSA method achieves superior reconstruction accuracy and forecasting performance relative to leading contemporary techniques.

Deep-learning-driven Automatic Essay Scoring (AES) tools have become increasingly popular, yet their internal evaluation mechanisms and decision logic remain largely obscure. This study offers insights into the operational characteristics of top AES contenders, specifically reviewing the HEPS v3.0 system used by the ETS Corporation and the Essay grading capabilities of the competitive DeepEssay model. An investigation reveals that these candidates primarily depend on semantic and syntactic features derived from their language, as well as topic-specific keywords, to generate scores. Furthermore, the study highlights critical operational characteristics shared among such systems: a pronounced topic effect where essays discussing the prompt are favored, and a topic saturation threshold where additional keyword usage can paradoxically lead to lower scores after a certain point. Although AES technologies continue to advance, these scholars note that the complex "topic effect" and saturation dynamics observed in leading models like HEPS v3.0 persist unchanged.

Microbial antagonizes offer a pathway to mitigate the adverse impacts often associated with standard chemical pesticide use. We propose a modeling framework for entomopathogenic nematodes, capturing their dual capability of harming host insects directly and suppressing host reproductive rates. While current detection and segmentation algorithms generally rely on gradient-based optimization to minimize the discrepancy between predicted and actual labels, these methods frequently become trapped in poor local minima, resulting in suboptimal performance. Pyroptosis serves as a crucial innate immune defense mechanism against microbial infections and underpins therapies for various inflammatory diseases; consequently, research into its regulatory pathways is expanding rapidly. The NLRP3 inflammasome, recognized as a primary driver of pyroptosis, has been the focus of this study, with an emphasis on reviewing recent advancements regarding its regulatory factors and inhibitors. By examining these recent developments, this review offers a comprehensive overview of regulatory mechanisms targeting the NLRP3 inflammasome, thereby facilitating a deeper understanding of pyroptosis and potentially informing the development of effective treatments for microbial infections and inflammatory disorders.

In reinforcement learning, exogenous state variables can introduce unpredictable variance into rewards, thereby decelerating the learning process. We provide a formal definition for these exogenous states and rewards, determining the conditions necessary to separate an exogenous Markov Reward Process (which incorporates only exogenous states and rewards) from the underlying endogenous Markov Decision Process (defined by endogenous rewards). Specifically, we formulate a variance-covariance criterion under which Monte Carlo policy evaluations on the endogenous component are more efficient than those applied to the full problem structure, with these efficiency gains extending broadly to reinforcement learning methodologies. Consequently, we present two distinct algorithms designed to detect these exogenous variables. Experimental results on various MDP tasks validate that these approaches are practically viable and deliver substantial accelerations in reinforcement learning performance.

Smart contracts automate agreement execution on blockchains and are increasingly adopted for critical financial and social purposes; however, verifying their correctness poses a significant challenge, potentially allowing costly and dangerous bugs to remain undetected. This paper introduces innovative techniques for formally verifying Solidity-based smart contracts using the Yulgen tool, which translates Solidity into low-target-independent Yulgen code. These methodologies ensure that computed outputs are error-free, that state transitions adhere strictly to intended logic, and that gas consumption stays within specified bounds, all while maintaining reasonable verification speeds.

Although Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNN) have demonstrated efficacy in solving various problems across computer science, particularly in computer vision and networking security, the pivotal role played by convolution layers within GCNN regarding feature extraction remains inadequately examined. This study reveals that a convolution layer in GCNN mathematically corresponds to applying an edge-based filter to graph functions, where the filter is defined by its frequency domain characteristics. Building upon this insight, we propose a methodology to design graph convolutions by first specifying a frequency domain edge filter and subsequently transforming it into the spatial domain. Employing this approach, we developed spatial domain design patterns for graph convolutions, which have been utilized to create efficient and precise solutions for node classification tasks in graphs with frequent structures, such as those found in computer vision and networking contexts. Computational analyses and graph-based classification experiments support the proposed framework, with results showing that the derived design patterns not only simplify spatial graph convolutions but also outperform or match state-of-the-art graph network models.

The study concerns a class of Einstein-Alexandrov fields defined by a requirement that the holonomy of specific connections remains trivial, where this triviality condition determines whether these fields admit non-trivial self-gravity. Within this framework, solutions corresponding to self-gravitating scalar solitons are derived and explicitly calculated for varying values of the scalar coupling. Additionally, the properties of de Sitt-like Einstein-Alexandrov geometries containing a cosmological constant, which satisfy the trivial holonomy condition, are explored within the same model.

We show that $\mathcal{N}=4$ supersymmetric Yang-Mills theories featuring the $${\mathfrak{so}(4N}}$$ Lie algebra and suitable global structures support non-invertible symmetries. Our approach involves identifying the condensing condensates of appropriate Lagrangian and vertex defects, which allow us to determine the complete fusion rules and identify the generators of the symmetry group. The structure of these defects reveals that the symmetries are primarily generated by the condensation of specific surface and line defects.

Ultrasound elastography represents a promising noninvasive method for visualizing tissue mechanical properties through color maps or animations. Speech Translation involves converting spoken audio in one language into written text in another. Although traditional machine translation techniques have achieved remarkable performance, the capability of zero-shot translation—where models generalize across languages they were not explicitly trained on using multilingual datasets—remains a significant challenge. In this research, we examine zero-shot speech translation using two specific corpora: the Microsoft Speech Corpora (MSR) and the Opus-1000 dataset. Our findings indicate that zero-shot speech translation presents substantially higher difficulty than the well-established zero-shot machine translation task. Furthermore, we observe a negative correlation between model performance and acoustic distance between source and target languages, suggesting that speech translation models inherently struggle more when bridging languages that are acoustically dissimilar compared to standard text-to-translation approaches.

Utilizing generative adversarial networks (GANs), disease-aware image editing represents a promising approach to constructing intelligent systems for medical diagnosis assistance. Specifically, StyleGAN plays a key role due to its ability to create highly realistic images, making it ideal for modifying medical image datasets to aid future diagnosis support through Augmentation by Adversarial Neural Networks. This study focuses on adapting StyleGAN for generating lung infection chest X-rays—a critical yet challenging task. Our strategy involves training the model using "smart" implicit labels, addressing the difficulty of obtaining explicit infection locations within these images. Our method isolates region-specific attributes, such as lung areas, from the rest of the image and utilizes them to supervise the generation of X-rays exhibiting artificial infections. These lung-infection XRays are then employed to retrain the entire diagnostic pipeline, encompassing both the encoding and decoding networks of the GAN model as well as the ultimate disease diagnosis head. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that our method successfully educates the entire end-to-end system to identify phantom infections, ultimately enhancing the model's performance on natural lung infection detection tasks. Extensive evaluations across three public datasets and ablation studies confirm the superiority of our proposed technique and its practical applicability.
